title: Shared infrastructure: Harvey proposes continuous client collaboration
desc: Moves from sequential reports toward reusable, permissioned workflows and self-service while leaving the lawyer’s agentic role incompletely specified.

kps.k: Harvey presents shared AI infrastructure as a way to redesign legal service delivery, not merely accelerate individual tasks.
kps.d: The central proposition is that firms, in-house teams and professional advisers can replace fragmented handoffs with joint analysis, shared workflows and continuous client engagement. Shared Spaces packages firm knowledge into client-accessible document collections, drafting workflows and negotiation guidance. Harvey argues that this model can strengthen firms’ relationships and differentiation while giving clients more immediate access to expertise; it does not establish changes in pricing or profitability.

kps.k: The proposed operational shift is from sequential reports to continuous, jointly developed work.
kps.d: In Harvey’s February 2026 article, PwC and IFS describe seeing deal issues and developing analysis in real time rather than waiting for final reports. Harvey extends this approach to shared diligence, litigation evidence and pleadings, ongoing compliance dialogue and access to dispersed governance records. Other design partners describe possibilities they are still exploring, rather than completed transformations. Practical implementation involves assigning review tasks, tracking ownership and combining lawyers’ legal analysis with clients’ business context.

kps.k: Client self-service and longer agentic workflows coexist with a continuing, but unevenly specified, lawyer role.
kps.d: Shared Spaces explicitly retains firm review of client-generated drafts and lawyer oversight of structured guidance. John LaBarre’s account of Harvey’s own legal team similarly describes lawyers using playbooks for familiar redlines and concentrating on novel issues. The May 2026 agent announcement makes a broader claim: more than 500 lawyer-built agents can carry longer processes through to client-ready files. Its obligation-tracking example still leaves subsequent action to the in-house team. The material contains no direct opposing argument; the important tension is between explicit augmentation workflows and end-to-end marketing that leaves verification requirements unspecified. Internal lawyer testing does not itself demonstrate reliability without human review.

kps.k: Permissions, confidentiality and workflow integration are central conditions of the collaboration model.
kps.d: Harvey describes administrator approval, granular resource permissions and audit logs as ways to share selected expertise without exposing all underlying materials. Its planned April 2026 Ansarada integration extends this logic to transaction data rooms: document exports require sell-side permission, and the companies promise synchronised content and permissions. Microsoft 365 integrations and mobile access seek to reduce tool-switching, while configurable workflows encode organisational precedents and logic. These accounts imply implementation work around testing, sharing boundaries and review ownership; the security and efficiency assurances are company claims, not independently validated results.

qs.q: Cross-organization collaboration can be configured to require admin approval, with granular, object-level permissions (e.g., view, comment, run, edit) to protect proprietary knowledge while keeping work moving.

kps.k: Harvey links reusable automation to flexible capacity for both corporate legal departments and lean firms.
kps.d: The argument is that teams can handle more document-heavy work without proportionate staffing increases and redirect experienced lawyers toward judgment and strategy. Harvey reports more than 18,000 custom workflows built after its June 2025 release, which indicates adoption rather than measured productivity. The mid-sized-firm account reports roughly 75% adoption among Moses Singer’s lawyers and staff, and attributes up to a 90% efficiency boost in selected document-review tasks and around seven hours saved per attorney weekly to B. Cremades & Asociados. These customer-reported results support a capacity argument in particular settings, not a general finding of lawyer replacement or firmwide margin improvement.

qs.q: Because AI tools like Harvey scale up and down as needed, firms can “flex” into heavier workloads — like that from an especially massive set of documents to review during diligence or discovery — without either scrambling to add staff or narrowing the scope of their analyses.

kps.k: The evidence supports reported adoption and perceived benefits more clearly than causal claims about service transformation.
kps.d: Harvey’s February 2026 article cites its RSGI report: more than 50% of law firms report faster delivery and better-quality service, 82% of in-house teams report increased capacity without added headcount, and 55% report rethinking law-firm collaboration. These figures concern Harvey generally, not a stated evaluation of Shared Spaces, which remained in early access with general availability expected in March 2026. Design-partner testimonials and illustrative workflows add operational detail but do not independently establish budget savings, accuracy or durable relationship gains. The supplied BigLaw Bench, Pathways Project and GPT-5.5 excerpts contain platform marketing rather than the research findings their titles suggest; repeated website copy and financing announcements add no performance validation.

vlens.an: The curated legal-tech-vendor sources support the proposition that shared, permissioned AI infrastructure can move legal service delivery beyond isolated task acceleration toward continuous collaboration, reusable workflows and client self-service. Their common rationale is that firms, in-house teams and other advisers can work from shared documents and analysis, reduce sequential handoffs, encode organisational expertise in workflows and playbooks, and preserve confidentiality through granular permissions and auditability. Most also retain a lawyer role in reviewing drafts, applying judgment and deciding next steps. There is material internal variation: product announcements focused on Shared Spaces directly advance the collaboration model; the legal-agent announcement builds a concrete agentic layer capable of longer, deliverable-producing workflows; the Ansarada partnership emphasises governed integration with transaction infrastructure; and the mid-sized-firm source redirects attention toward flexible internal capacity, staffing and margins rather than firm–client collaboration. The evidence is also uneven: detailed workflow descriptions, company-reported adoption and customer testimonials support feasibility and perceived benefits more clearly than causal claims about durable service-model transformation. Several marketing extracts assert end-to-end execution without specifying verification, while Shared Spaces materials explicitly preserve lawyer oversight. These sources are predominantly Harvey’s own first-party claims and should not be treated as representative of legal-tech vendors generally.

elens.an: The 2023–2024 source supports the proposition at a broad, promotional level. It presents Harvey as shared infrastructure through which legal teams can work securely across organisational boundaries and claims that firms and professional-services networks are already using the platform to develop collaborative service models. This anticipates the later cluster synthesis’s shift from isolated task acceleration toward redesigned, jointly delivered legal services. The source also pairs collaboration with end-to-end agents intended to leave lawyers focused on distinctively legal work, broadly aligning with augmentation. However, it does not describe continuous client collaboration, reusable permissioned workflows, review ownership or verification in operational detail, and it supplies no independent evidence that service delivery was transformed. Because the extract is largely product copy attached to a 2023 funding post, its claims should not be treated as validated results or as representative of the wider period. These limitations qualify the strength of support but do not create substantive opposition.

elens.an:
The curated 2025 sources support the proposition that Harvey’s shared AI infrastructure can move legal service delivery from isolated task acceleration and sequential handoffs toward reusable workflows, client self-service and continuous firm–client collaboration. Common reasons include embedding firm knowledge in repeatable Playbooks and Workflows, bringing clients and lawyers into shared document environments, preserving lawyer review of client-generated work, and using permissions, audit trails and task ownership to control cross-organisation collaboration. The sources also report signs of adoption, including extensive internal use, more than 18,000 customer-built workflows and integration into existing tools, but these usage figures demonstrate uptake rather than causal service transformation.

There is material variation in scope and evidential strength. The internal legal-team account principally demonstrates augmentation within Harvey and only anticipates outside-counsel collaboration. The Shared Spaces announcement and product retrospective describe the collaboration model in operational detail, including self-service, parallel review, verification and access controls. The financing announcement supports the direction only through broad promotional claims about new service models. Across the period, the evidence is entirely first-party Harvey material: it provides product capabilities, company-reported adoption and illustrative workflows, but not independent validation of accuracy, budget savings, profitability or durable relationship gains. The lawyer’s role is clearer in first-draft review and contextual verification than in broader claims about end-to-end agentic workflows. Because these are curated company sources, their alignment should not be treated as evidence of wider consensus or prevalence.

elens.an: The curated 2026 sources overall support the proposition that Harvey is moving legal AI beyond isolated task acceleration toward shared, permissioned infrastructure for continuous collaboration among law firms, in-house teams and other professional advisers. The common rationale is operational: participants can work from the same materials, observe analysis as it develops, reuse workflows, and integrate AI into document-heavy matters while permissions, auditability and governance protect sensitive information. Several sources also retain a role for lawyers or in-house teams in strategic judgment and subsequent decisions. Material variation concerns emphasis and evidentiary strength. The Shared Spaces article most directly supports real-time joint work; the legal-agents announcement builds on it by extending automation into longer, deliverable-producing workflows; and the Ansarada partnership supplies a concrete governed integration with transaction infrastructure. Repeated platform excerpts endorse the proposition but are promotional copy rather than benchmark or research findings. The mid-sized-firm source redirects attention from cross-organisational collaboration to internal capacity, staffing flexibility and margins. Across the selection, claimed transformation is supported more clearly as a product vision, adoption claim and set of reported experiences than as an independently validated causal outcome: several benefits are prospective, Shared Spaces was in early access, and the human verification required for end-to-end agentic work remains incompletely specified.
